Tech Report: ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’: Inside the Psychedelic 1970s-Inspired Dystopian Sets

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1790 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins.
  • Lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena.
  • District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Francis Lawrence, director of The Hunger Games, has a tradition with author Suzanne Collins. Before bringing a new installment of her bestselling dystopian saga to the big screen, the two join forces to envision how the fictional world of Panem will take shape. “I go to New York each time, and we sit in a conference room at Scholastic,” indicates Lawrence, who has directed five of the franchise’s six films. “We go through the book page by page and beat out what we think the movie is going to look like.”.

Lawrence’s latest adaptation, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping (in theaters today), returns to Panem, a postapocalyptic nation where the ruling Capitol controls twelve districts through extreme systemic oppression—most notoriously the titular spectacle in which children are selected by lottery and forced to fight to the death in an arena. Set twenty-four years before the original The Hunger Games (2012) plotline, the prequel follows District 12’s sixteen-year-old Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada)—the future mentor (played by Woody Harrelson) to Katniss Everdeen (Jennifer Lawrence) and Peeta Mellark (Josh Hutcherson)—as he is selected to fight in the Second Quarter Quell, a particularly sadistic rendition of the Games held every twenty-five years.

District 12’s female tribute Maysilee Donner (McKenna Grace) at the reaping.

Though the dystopia is set in a future North America, the previous prequel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes (2023), drew from the architecture of 1940s and ’50s postwar Berlin to depict evil President Snow’s rise to tyranny. Set forty years later, Sunrise explores Panem at a newly introduced stage of its evolution. Designed by returning production designer Uli Hanisch, the film follows Haymitch from his impoverished mining district, which barely evolves throughout the series’s sixty-five year timeline, to the opulent Capitol, whose extravagance is expressed through a 1970s-inflected visual lexicon.

“I realized the ’70s fall right smack in the middle between that movie and the originals, so we could lean into that,” states Lawrence. Hanisch and his team incorporated references to Andy Warhol, Studio 54, and the decade’s psychedelic color palette, appropriating its progressive spirit to convey the Capitol’s opulence and authoritarianism—and, particularly in the arena, using the aesthetic as a means of deception. “To turn the ’70s style from something progressive, liberal, young, and open-minded into something evil is a twist,” says Hanisch. “But that is the key to the entire film’s design.”.

Haymitch and Maysilee as allies in the arena. The forest portion was filmed separately near Cologne, Germany.

Recent findings suggest that the stylistic choice is also a poignant nod to Collins’s original inspiration for the book series. The 1970s marked a transformation in American television: as color TVs became ubiquitous in households across the country, sporting spectacles, variety reveals, and beauty pageants flourished, establishing cultural touchstones that would help shape the contemporary reality programming Collins critiques and satirizes in The Hunger Games. “I was flipping through the channels one night between reality television programs and actual footage of the Iraq War, when the idea came to me,” Collins recalled in a 2018 interview with The New York Times. The juxtaposition inspired her to explore just-war theory for young people through an authoritarian dystopia in which mass entertainment is an instrument of political control.

From an abandoned rural steel mill to authoritarian monuments from postwar Berlin, the film draws on politically charged German sites to capture Panem at a pivotal stage in its political and architectural evolution.

Sources indicate that production Designer Uli Hanisch at the District 12 set. “District 12 is the most sentimental set to me because I’d known this site near my hometown my entire life,” Hanisch notes.

To recreate the Appalachian-inspired, deteriorating industrial landscape of District 12 that was shot in Atlanta in the original series, the production utilized a sprawling abandoned steel mill in Duisburg, Germany, Hanisch’s hometown. “I wish we had it in the original movies, because it is an unbelievable space,” Lawrence claims of the post-industrial, rural landscape, which also appeared in The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, Hanisch’s first film in the franchise. “Everywhere you look is exactly how I have always imagined District 12.”.

Recent findings suggest that while District 12 was filmed near Atlanta in the original films, director Francis Lawrence’s fascination with German architecture brought production to Berlin for The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. It was there that he began collaborating with Berlin-based production designer Hanisch, who proposed this steel mill nearby his hometown for the newly introduced location. Upon seeing photographs, Lawrence exclaimed, “Are you kidding me? ... Let’s go tomorrow,” and promptly flew out to see it for himself.

The production designer added modest huts at the edge of a nearby quarry to recreate the Seam, home to Haymitch, his girlfriend Lenore Dove (Whitney Peak), and fellow tribute Louella McCoy (Molly McCann), its humble dwellings contrasting the more prosperous merchant district inhabited by fellow tribute Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace).

“Unlike the Capitol, District 12 doesn't evolve stylistically throughout the films. Nobody is investing in it, and everything is gradually deteriorating,” Hanisch explains. The vivid purples and oranges of the Capitol’s ‘70s palette are notably absent, only appearing prominently in propaganda decorating the reaping square, including Hunger Games campaign materials and posters portraying Snow as Panem’s number-one Peacekeeper.

Druscilla in the Capitol before the tribute interviews, which is broadcast to all of Panem.

In the Capitol, however, the architecture takes on a distinctly ‘70s flair. Rooted in the Roman concept of panem et circenses, or “bread and circuses,” from which Panem takes its name, the architecture reinforces the government’s manipulation through spectacle. In the background is Berlin's International Congress Centrum, a colossal, aluminum-clad convention center that opened in 1979, which Lawrence describes as “Cold War-era Berlin showing off in a modern way.” As West Berlin’s most expensive postwar building, the futuristic complex was publicly subsidised to showcase economic prosperity and technological advancement—an evocative backdrop for the Capitol’s own display of authoritarianism.

“It’s a time of peace for the Capitol with no rebel attacks, so Snow's had time to build the city up in a way that is an extravagant show of power,” Lawrence explains. The chariot parade, which introduces the tributes before the Games, similarly unfolds against the historically-charged Berlin Olympiastadion, which was designed by Werner March for the 1936 Olympics under Nazi Germany to project state power and an illusion of timeless permanence.

In a recent development, the upstairs library in Plutarch’s home, which he inherited from the Heavensbee dynasty. Reflecting the Capitol’s classic style, it contrasts the Plutarch’s modern downstairs salon which features Warhol-inspired portraits, including one of director Lawrence.

It has been revealed that the Capitol's grandeur is also exhibited inside the mansion of Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons), a cameraman with historic ties to Panem’s ruling class. “This was one of my favorite sets because of the scope and scale” Lawrence claims, noting how its excess reflects the dynasty's immense wealth. Filmed at Berlin's late-1960s modernist Congress Center, the circular residence required twenty-five vans of retro-modern furniture to fill it. The salon, decked in vibrant 1970s furnishings and Warhol-inspired art, showcases Plutarch's modern sensibilities, in stark contrast to the upstairs library inherited from his family. “We wanted to distinguish Plutarch from the dynasty he comes from,” Lawrence explains, reflecting on how the expansive volumes must be a facade of intellectual sophistication.

It has been revealed that the set decoration department spent weeks hand-folding and assembling thousands of hollow cardboard books, interspersed with real volumes, including a collection of Edgar Allan Poe’s poetry, which Plutarch references to Haymitch. “We imagined Plutarch might actually be the first Heavensbee to read some of those books,” Hanisch indicates. “He even says the library is one of the few worthwhile things his ancestors accomplished.”.

According to recent reports, the library's custom-built curved bookshelves envelope the characters, symbolising the insularity of Capitol society. “Circles represent both inclusion and exclusion,” Hanisch states. “If you are in the circle, you're in. And if you're not, you're out.” As fans of the franchise will know, Plutarch (originally played by Philip Seymour Hoffman) later reveals himself as a double agent and leader of the underground rebellion against Snow’s regime.

Industry observers note that the aspect ratio expands as Haymitch ascends into the eye-shaped arena, emphasizing the landscape’s immersive scale and beauty. While scouting locations, Lawrence drew inspiration from the dramatic landscapes in Terrence Malick’s A Hidden Life. “I had that in my head, only it was a little trippier. The Asturias were perfect,” he recalls. The kaleidoscopic design also inspired the official logo of the 50th Hunger Games, extending the arena’s psychedelic imagery into the Capitol’s propaganda.

The Quarter Quell arena, in particular, embodies the surreal, fantastical ethos of the 1970s that permeates the film, illustrating how the Capitol exploits beauty to disguise its underlying manipulation and brutality. “As I was reading with Suzanne, I noted there was an Alice in Wonderland-like element to it, which made me think of the song ‘White Rabbit,’ which made me think of the late ’60s, early ’70s,” Lawrence recalls. “That kind of broke something open for me.”.

In a recent development, designed in the shape of an eye, the eight to ten mile arena serves as a metaphor for the Capitol's omnipresent surveillance. A golden Cornucopia forms its pupil; vibrant meadows its iris; and the surrounding mountain ranges its whites. In the book, Haymitch describes the especially lethal arena masquerading as an idyllic landscape as a “poisonous beauty of an arena.”.

Industry observers note that lawrence and Haymitch in the arena. The physical flowers were concentrated in the foreground, while visual effects extended the colorful landscape into the distance.

Seeking to capture as much natural landscape as possible, Hanisch and location manager Klaus große Darrelmann discovered a remote valley in Asturias, Spain, surrounded by the Cantabrian Mountains. Transforming the isolated valley into a psychedelic paradise proved an enormous undertaking.“The arena was our nemesis,” states Hanisch, recalling how the production had to bring extensive resources to the remote terrain. “You can't even imagine how far away it was or how hard it was to get to.” Crews spent weeks individually installing hundreds of thousands of artificial flowers throughout the meadows and forests.

It has been revealed that despite the arena’s dreamlike beauty, water sources, flowers, and vegetation conceal deadly poisons. “It’s the most colorful and playful dystopia you’ll ever see,” producer Nina Jacobson says. Perhaps more than anywhere else in Panem, the arena encapsulates how the Capitol weaponizes the electric zeitgeist of the ‘70s as an instrument of control. “To have something so overwhelmingly beautiful and seductive but poisonous and deadly is very cruel,” Hanisch says. “That contradiction captures the mentality of Panem at this point in its history.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volkswagen will reveal the new GTI hot hatch on Friday, promising it will be “something really spicy.”.

To celebrate the GTI’s 50th anniversary, Volkswagen is “starting a upcoming chapter,” with its first all-electric model to bear the iconic performance badge.

The ID. Polo GTI “brings the legendary GTI driving pleasure into the electric future,” VW said after opening pre-orders last month.

In a recent development, volkswagen previewed a mysterious new hot hatch draped under a cloth that appears to be a souped-up version of the ID. Polo GTI. Despite its attempt to “hide” it, you can see the massive rear wing and wide wheel arches under the cloth.

The manufacturer promised that “something really spicy” will be served this Friday, November 20, with the tags #Volkswagen, #GTI, and #GTI50.

Although no other details were revealed, the newly introduced hot hatch is thought to be the more powerful “Clubsport” variant.

A post shared by Volkswagen (@volkswagen).

Recent findings suggest that volkswagen’s head of driving dynamics, Florian Umbach, told Autocar earlier this year that the company is planning to launch the ID. Polo GTI Clubsport, a more powerful variant that will deliver close to 300 hp, up from 223 hp in the standard model.

Umbach mentioned that Volkswagen is developing “a similar kind of paddleshift power delivery that the Hyundai N cars have” for the upcoming electric hot hatch.

Recent findings suggest that hyundai’s performance EVs, the IONIQ 5 N and IONIQ 6 N, feature a simulated gear-shifting system called N e-Shift that uses paddle shifters on the steering wheel to replicate the feel of an 8-speed dual-clutch transmission. It works with the N Active Sound+ system to make it feel like you’re in a traditional gas-powered sports car.

In a recent development, it has yet to be confirmed whether the hot hatch debuting on Friday is, in fact, the new ID. Polo Clubsport, but the design clues give us a good idea of what’s coming.

In a recent development, man, $45k for a starting price is a little uncomfortably steep for a hatch, given there are a little bigger options in that range. I wish it started somewhere in the 30s to be competitive.

Check back on Friday for the full details.

Volkswagen opened pre-orders for the ID. Polo GTI last month, starting at 39,995 euros (about $45,000).

In a recent development, like the first Golf GTI from 1976, the electric ID. Polo GTI uses a front-wheel-drive powertrain. The front-mounted electric motor delivers 223 hp (166 kW) and 213 lb-ft (290 Nm) of instant torque, enabling it to sprint from 0 to 62 mph (0 to 100 km/h) in 6.8 seconds.

In early 2027, Volkswagen will open orders for the ID.3 GTI, the second EV to wear the badge, and its first rear-wheel-drive (RWD) GTI.

#98652. I’ve Weighed the Same for 7 Years. My Body Has Changed Completely.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (893 w)

I’ve Weighed the Same for 7 Years. My Body Has Changed Completely.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (893 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • A FEW MONTHS ago, my friend Jack Espy stopped by Men’s Health HQ, and as we were talking shop and swapping stories with MH senior editor Ryan Brower about our favorite fitness-workout-wellness gear, I asked them both to name their single favorite product.
  • Jack chose his Garmin watch and raved about its amazing battery life.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

A FEW MONTHS ago, my friend Jack Espy stopped by Men’s Health HQ, and as we were talking shop and swapping stories with MH senior editor Ryan Brower about our favorite fitness-workout-wellness gear, I asked them both to name their single favorite product.

Jack chose his Garmin watch and raved about its amazing battery life. Ryan named his Adidas Adizero Evo SL running shoes. As for me? It was hard: the one thing, among allll the things, that actually moves the needle? After thinking for a full 20 seconds, it finally hit me:.

Weird and kind of random, right?

According to recent reports, I thought so, too. I’ve never cared that much about how much I weigh, mostly because I didn’t have to and I didn’t want to. I’ve always been on the leaner side, so for most of my adult life, the extent of what I knew about my weight came down to whether my pants fit.

Then, about a decade ago, I started getting more serious about putting on muscle, and my trainer at the time, the substantial-armed and bigger-brained David Otey, introduced me to a kind of body-composition testing, a.k.a. “bioelectrical impedance analysis,” or BIA. The tech has been used to estimate body composition for decades, and you’ve probably seen one of the more sophisticated machines at your gym or doctor’s office. Step onto a platform, grab a pair of handles, wait 30 seconds, and the machine spits out a breakdown of how much of you is body fat, skeletal muscle mass, and more.

David walked me through how BIA works: The machine sends a teeny-tiny electrical current through your body. Electricity moves more easily through lean tissue than through fat, so by measuring how that current travels through you, the machine can estimate how much fat and muscle you’re carrying.

It has been revealed that in 2019, I bought an InBody Dial H20N for my bathroom. By then, BIA was well established in the consumer “smart scale” market, and InBody’s scale was among the more advanced at-home options, using sensors at both your hands and feet to take a more complete reading of your body than the foot-only models that were common at the time. The app tracks every measurement, so I can see not just what my body looks like on any given day but how it has changed over time.

To understand why I love the damn thing, it’s important to know that I weigh roughly the same today as when I first brought the scale home seven years ago.

A conventional (dumb) scale would look at seven years of strength training, workouts I wanted to skip, workouts I probably should have skipped, and a totally unreasonable amount of thought about what I put into my body and deliver its verdict: Congrats, you weigh the same!

But the InBody tells a different story. When I look back at my results from 2019, it estimated that I carried about 84 pounds of skeletal muscle mass and 33 pounds of body fat. Today, it indicates I’ve got around 95 pounds of skeletal muscle and 24 pounds of body fat. Yep: According to the scale, I’ve added 11 pounds of muscle while losing about 9 pounds of fat—all while my total body weight has barely moved. (I won’t mention that I did all this during a stage of life when building muscle, and simply holding on to it, gets harder than it was when I was 25. But I will mention Men’s Health has done an amazing guide to body recomposition that is worth checking out.).

According to recent reports, now, a necessary reality check: Those body-comp numbers aren’t exact measurements in the same way that the number staring back at me from a dumb scale is a measurement. They’re estimates. My hydration levels can throw them off. What I just ate can throw them off. A hard workout can really throw them off.

Still, in studies comparing the InBody to much fancier ways of measuring body composition, the scale holds up surprisingly well for something that lives in your bathroom. There’s even a upcoming model, the H40, that Inbody says is even more precise. (I keep meaning to buy it, but then something breaks in my house and a new scale gets knocked down the priority list.).

It has been revealed that none of this means that I obsess over whether I have 94.7 pounds of muscle on Tuesday and 93.9 on Thursday. What makes this useful to me aren’t the exact numbers; it’s the direction they’re headed in. I still don’t really care how much I weigh—I wear the same pants size as when I was 25 and 35, and all my blood work is fine. But I’m trying to carry more muscle, less fat, and a stronger, more capable body into the second half of my life. I just want to know that some of my ass-busting efforts are paying off.

A dumb scale can’t tell me that. But a smart scale—this smart scale—is giving me all the direction I need.

FIND THE INBODY DIAL H20 ON AMAZON.

Richard Dorment is the editorial director of Men’s Health and Women’s Health.

In the Berkshires, an Intensely Yellow Kitchen Is Anything but Mellow in This Lakeside Cottage

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1388 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Architecturaldigest

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, “I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” says Jess Cooney.
  • Cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea.
  • According to recent reports, cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “I personally would not want this yellow in my kitchen,” says Jess Cooney. It’s a cheeky comment about the beaming hue she herself chose for clients in the Berkshires—a color that defines their entire lakeside home, one she calls the diva of the whole project, requiring (no, demanding) decisions in every square foot to balance out its intensity.

Cooney’s clients didn’t blink at the bold idea. Unusually carefree for a couple with high-powered jobs, they gave the AD PRO Directory designer free license to create. The bungalow was purchased as a weekend retreat from life in New York, but even before paint swatches were discussed, the kitchen was a sticking point. “The kitchen was crazy—it was this tiny little makeshift kitchen,” claims Cooney.

According to recent reports, cooney’s clients weren’t initially convinced by reclaimed brick flooring in the entryway, but Cooney’s team proved convincing—they believed the space needed a worn palette to counterbalance the intensely yellow kitchen. Much to their clients’ delight, it worked beautifully. A Croft House Morro Credenza with leather-front doors anchors the space, topped with a vintage lamp from Millerton Antiques Center and set beneath an unknown artwork from Brimfield Flea Market.

Cooney opted to stain wood-paneled walls in custom blue and brown stains from Rubio Monocoat, allowing rustic grains to shine through. Atop a Jaipur Hazan rug, an upholstered George Smith Emma Ottoman anchors the room and is accompanied by a set of armchairs and a velvet mordoré sofa from Lawson-Fenning. A 20th-century oil painting by Paul Berg hangs above the reworked fireplace, while in the corner, above a Charles Dudouyt side table, hangs a vintage painting sourced from The Little Store in Massachusetts.

Recent findings suggest that “We just decided to kind of lean into it and go almost in a maximalist way,” says Cooney of the dining room’s focal point, a painting by K.G. Narendra Babu that inspired the home’s many colors. For the inside of a Four Hands Camila Sideboard, they commissioned artisan Joel Haynes to hand-paint a leafy pattern. A Hubbardton Forge Disq fixture hangs above a custom Bossi dining table surrounded with Tribute Modern Dining Chairs from Craft Associates.

The husband, an English lawyer, craved a small cabin in the woods, while the wife, an Italian who loves cooking, wanted a home large enough to host intimate gatherings. “This house was a happy compromise,” notes the husband. But while the home spans three levels and around 4,500 square feet, the main floor measured just about 1,000. The kitchen, in a cramped corner, didn’t cut it.

Sources indicate that cooney’s team reconfigured a few walls. They collapsed oversized closets in the entryway, shrinking the space to a slimmer mudroom while letting the entire layout exhale, expanding the footprint of the semi-open cooking area. The room is now the proper heart of the home, and its bright yellow cabinets aren’t shy about it.

Cabinets with glass windows were fabricated by Westek Architectural Woodworking and feature an array of white porcelain that punctuates and calms the intensely painted millwork; the pieces were all sourced from shops in the Berkshires, including Millerton Antiques, All that Jazz, and Montage Antiques.

“It’s the diva of the project,” claims Cooney of the yellow Benjamin Moore paint used throughout the kitchen, a choice that influenced nearly all palettes throughout the home. Ceilings, walls, and upper cabinets were painted in Farrow & Ball’s Newly introduced White.

Sources indicate that the kitchen island is topped with a wooden counter and is paired with Amber Interiors Cade Counter Stools in walnut. A set of Matthew Fairbank Allegro Pendants hang above the island.

The saturated hue, Benjamin Moore’s Glen Ridge Gold, wasn’t a choice made on a whim. Like many colors peppering the home, it was inspired by a painting by Chennai-based artist K.G. Narendra Babu that now hangs in the couple’s dining room. The artwork was given to the couple by a family member who worked in India, and it features an array of folk and musical motifs.

According to recent reports, “The whole point of the project is that it’s bright and energetic and deeply relaxing at the same time,” says Cooney. “That was the trust that they put in us—to believe that both could happen.”.

The architecture itself lacked a definitive style. Light traces of Arts & Crafts style gave Cooney a point of view to reinvent existing character. A fireplace in the living room is now reimagined with glazed brick Clé tiles, their dappled surface cladding the surround with clean lines and a crafted look; a custom stain allowed wood-paneled walls to bear rustic grains but in modern blue-green tones.

Recent findings suggest that to expand the kitchen’s footprint, Cooney reclaimed space from unnecessarily large closets in the entryway. Her team moved the wall to install smaller, but equally useful, cabinets that turn the space into a mudroom. The custom millwork, crafted by Westek Architectural Woodworking and painted in Farrow & Ball’s Blue Gray, complements a vintage rug and a built-in bench.

A custom walnut vanity injects warmth as an alternative to a colder stone. Cooney’s team used a boat sealer to coat and protect the walnut, giving the material a high-gloss finish. A fabric shade made with Eric Kuster’s Micha 002 textile occupies the space that might traditionally feature a mirror. “You can kind of break a rule and have it be playful and fun, especially in a powder bath,” says Cooney, noting that a mirror hangs on the side wall instead. The wallcovering is Pierre Frey’s Uberon print.

Cooney describes an almost cottagey feel in the primary, thanks to a walnut Flora Bed by Jacob May, which was locally made and turned by hand, layered with cozy and textural textiles like Parachute Home’s Hand Stitched Cotton Quilt. Gentle patterns add to the mix through a Scandinavian kilim with geometric design from Rug & Kilim, and light drapes made with a Best Buds textile by Kerry Joyce.

It has been revealed that making the most of existing features, light touches to the bathroom reimagined the space, like painting existing wainscoting in Farrow & Ball’s Tanner’s Brown, and covering the walls in a botanical House of Hackney Herbarium wallpaper. For a touch of texture, Cooney also layered vintage rugs and set an antique Victorian bamboo chair in the corner below the window.

Recent findings suggest that with a view over the living room, Cooney says the lofted floor is like a little escape within the small cottage. Leaning into the cozy feel, the team went with a layered look. A brass chest anchors the space, paired with a black armchair owned by the clients, which was reupholstered with a burgundy fabric from Abraham Moon & Sons, and a Lawson-Fenning Morro Sectional in a linen blend.

In a recent development, the clients’ only real hesitation was a bit of a surprise: the reclaimed brick Cooney specified for the mudroom. It is laid in a herringbone pattern with colors that appeared to shift across the surface. That yellow kitchen? Totally fine. But the expressive bricks? Too dramatic. “We relied on the team’s judgement, and this feature is now one of our most favorite parts of the home,” says the husband, noting how guests often compliment the mudroom.

Sources indicate that “I feel like this house is kind of us unchecked,” says Cooney of her clients’ trust. “No one checked us, so we were allowed to do the fullest extent of what we wanted to do.” Her clients could easily have staged their own diva moment after the cabinets were painted in screaming yellow, before everything else around it fell into place around it; but they let the vision come into full focus.

As if cantilevered over the hill, a screened-in porch is the best of both worlds. “You don’t have to have everything be indoor-outdoor in a covered porch—you can really pull the inside out there and not worry so much,” says Cooney, nodding to choices like Henning Kjaernulf dining chairs from the 1960s purchased from Lone Fox. And while most might use a lighter color in this space, Cooney chose a deeper Farrow & Ball Hopper Head paint for the walls and window frames, which she says helps punctuate the view in a beautiful way.

The view overlooking the Berkshires.

#98648. Latest Update: How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2178 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Womenshealthmag ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: How Sculpt Became the Fitness Space’s Buzziest—and Vaguest—Workout

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Womenshealthmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay.
  • Over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture.
  • Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By definition, the term sculpt means making something by carving stone or molding clay. It’s an art form, a manipulation of material to achieve a desired end result that’s aesthetically appealing.

Over the years, however, the term has also become ubiquitous in fitness culture. We talk about sculpting one's back or legs, implying some kind of crafting of muscles, as if treating the human form like a sculpture. In fact, check the group class schedule of any gym these days, and you’ll likely spot the term “sculpt” appear somewhere on the lineup—directing toward some variation of a Pilates mat or strength training class, often involving lower weights and higher reps.

Now, the term is prolific in fitness classes and social media alike, that the meaning is a bit murky—which begs the question, what does “sculpt” really mean in the context of exercise? Is it a legitimate term or nothing more than strategic marketing language?

The exercise term actually dates back decades, with the first mentions appearing in fitness publications in the late 1970s. “It comes out of bodybuilding culture, which became more prominent in that period […] and you started to see the term ‘body sculpture,’” says Natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, a historian and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. And while there’s no clear record of who coined the term in a fitness context, there is speculation that it may have been inspired by German strongman Eugen Sandow (often called the "father of modern bodybuilding"), who referenced Greco-Roman sculptures as examples of the “ideal” physique in the late 19th century.

In the 1980s, the idea of sculpting your muscles started to become much more mainstream, with the rise of aerobics, toning workouts, and fitness videos, indicates physical therapist and trainer Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, founder of Evlo Fitness. As instructors began using the term to describe and market workouts designed to shape and define specific muscles, “sculpting” became part of the everyday fitness vocabulary.

It has been revealed that the term also taps into something more personal: this idea that we have the power to change the shape of our own physiques. “I think that it really gained momentum because one, it kind of speaks to the artistry of the body or the artistry of fitness. Also, there's so much individual agency in this,” states Petrezela. “It isn't about you just having the right genetics. Instead, you as an artist have the power to sculpt your own body.”.

According to recent reports, in the 1990s, however, the revered muscular look brought about by ’80s fitness culture made way for a celebration of thinner, more waifish bodies. “There was—and this is still the case—a lot of fear around getting too bulky,” says Petrezela. The term sculpting, however, molded into a promise of strength training without gaining too much muscle, which felt more palatable to women who feared such a physique.

“What's interesting is that we've changed the language over the years, but we're still selling women a very similar idea: that certain exercises will create a long, lean, toned appearance, while others will make them bulky,” indicates Ritchey.

If you worked out in the 2010s, you probably remember “sculpt” becoming a fixture of the boutique fitness boom. Still, while studio culture has waxed and waned over the last 20 years, the term has only gained traction, popping up across social media and on class schedules everywhere (think Pilates sculpt, yoga sculpt, and seemingly endless variations), notes Laura Girard, CPT, a NASM personal trainer and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Girard speculates that the popularity of sculpt classes may be buoyed by the widespread craving for more community in a post-pandemic world. After all, group fitness can be a fantastic third space. But there's another reason “sculpt” makes for such an appealing class name: It signals a particular kind of workout experience. Girard has observed “sculpt” used “almost like a dog whistle that [suggests] this class is going to be friendly for women and not scary, but still intense,” she notes.

Recent findings suggest that there's an aesthetic appeal, too. Petrezela believes the term’s resurgence of sorts has to do with how weightlifting and building muscle are very much having a moment, yet longstanding fears around getting “bulky” haven’t entirely disappeared. “It doesn't hurt that we are in a very, very image-driven moment in fitness culture,” she indicates. “We're not just looking at the images in magazines that come out once a month, but our [social media] feeds are nonstop bodies all day—many of which are shared by influencers who have their own plans for how you can sculpt a body that looks just like theirs, or so they say.”.

If you were to ask 10 different people on the street what a “sculpt class” is, you may get 10 different answers. To some, sculpt is synonymous with a mat Pilates routine, to others it might be a strength-training session, and to others it might be a yoga practice involving light dumbbells. So, can all of these workouts really fall under the same umbrella? And when a class promises to “sculpt,” is that an actual measurable result your muscles can deliver—or a feeling the name is designed to sell?

According to recent reports, according to the experts, it’s largely the latter. “In a world where two things are popular—strength training and being very thin—’sculpting’ seems to be an appealing middle ground from a marketing perspective,” says Ritchey. “It promises ‘long, lean muscle tone’ without the perceived risk of building too much muscle.”.

She adds that “sculpt” is often used interchangeably with “toning,” which she describes as a “made-up term” that typically refers to changing your body composition (a.k.a., reducing fat and building muscle).

Because there's no single definition, what you actually do in a sculpt class can vary considerably. Still, Girard notes many sculpt classes share certain characteristics: lighter weights, choreography-inspired movements, and a lot of mat work. She also notes that while exercises are often fatiguing (think: that familiar muscle-burning sensation), they’re not necessarily pushing you to muscle failure via progressive overload (which is necessary for hypertrophy, or muscle-building).

Industry observers note that ritchey, who taught a sculpt class years ago, recalls using dumbbells and bodyweight for high reps. “We would do an entire three- to four-minute song of squats and lunges. That’s likely over 100 squats in a row, which burns and feels hard,” she says. Of course, it’s certainly possible to promote muscle-building with a low-weight, high-rep range, granted the programming is intentional. “But we know that if you could physically do more than about 30 reps in a row, the load is too light to build muscle.”.

It’s vital to note that a workout doesn't have to maximize muscle growth to be worthwhile. Certain sculpt classes can offer other benefits, from muscular endurance to simply providing motivation and enjoyment of exercising, often in a group setting. But if your primary goal is to significantly increase muscle size or change your body composition, not every sculpt class will provide the progressive resistance training needed to make that happen.

Recent findings suggest that that’s where experts say the “sculpt” terminology can get confusing or misleading for some people. Girard fears that the language surrounding sculpt workouts reinforces misconceptions about women's bodies and what exercise can realistically change. “Sculpt as a verb is not a thing we can do to our bodies,” she notes. “We can gain or lose muscle. We can gain or lose fat, but that's more the role of nutrition. But we can't control how those muscles look.”.

Industry observers note that in other words, there's no special exercise technique that creates “long, lean” muscles instead of so-called “bulky” ones. Your genetics influence your muscle shape, while your training can affect how much muscle you build. And the workout's name doesn't change those underlying principles.

Industry observers note that what’s more, at a time when there’s seemingly no consensus on how to talk about bodies or fitness in an empowering, nonoffensive way, Girard sees the term “sculpt” as potential coded language. While we may have mostly done away with, say, “bikini body shred” language in 2026, she fears that this nebulous term may be subliminally hinting at the same idea.

And while there's absolutely “nothing wrong with having aesthetic goals,” Ritchey stresses, “women deserve accurate information about how to achieve them.” If body recomp is their goal, they would have more success lifting close to failure and focusing on diet.”.

Ultimately, your muscles don’t know whether you’re in a sculpt class or a traditional strength workout. Instead, they respond to the resistance, effort, and progression involved.

Sources indicate that “It’s funny because while all these trends come and go—and we will see sculpt come and go, too—the science never changes,” Ritchey states. “People just aren’t patient enough with the basics, so they jump on the latest trend thinking it will finally be the golden ticket to seeing results.”.

Because “sculpt” has no one definition, the quality, intensity, and overall experience of classes bearing the name can vary widely, too.

Beyond the workout itself, Girard points out that some sculpt classes can come with an unspoken expectation about who belongs in the room. As she’s observed: “These classes tend to be a self-selecting in-group. You may only see one type of body, or one specific outfit [...] That doesn’t mean it’s wrong or bad to be in a different outfit or in a different body, but it sure can feel that way.”.

Of course, there are also plenty of classes with “sculpt” in the name that are fantastic, inclusive workouts. This all boils down to the instructor, methods, and specific exercises they choose to incorporate—along with the type of community they cultivate. And, in many cases—particularly with larger studios or gyms—instructors have no say in what their class is actually called. “A lot of times, they're just doing what's trending to get people in the door,” states Girard.

It has been revealed that so if you’ve been curious to try a fresh sculpt class at a local studio—by all means, go for it. Just be sure to go into it with eyes wide open, and give yourself permission to stop or pause or walk away if it doesn’t feel like a productive or positive environment for you. Pay attention to how the workout feels, how the instructor coaches, and whether the environment makes you feel welcome. One potential red flag? Aggressive “bikini body” messaging or marketing that frames building muscle as something to avoid. As Girard emphasizes, “It is definitely, definitely is not.”.

As the experts agree: Finding a form of movement you enjoy is the most important ingredient for establishing a healthy, consistent fitness routine. “My advice would be to ask yourself why you're doing these classes. Is it because you genuinely enjoy them? Or is it because you believe the burning sensation means you're toning and sculpting your muscles? Because those are two very different things,” indicates Ritchey.

Have a sculpt workout you absolutely love? That’s wonderful, too. Finding movement you genuinely enjoy is one of the best ways to build a fitness routine you'll actually stick with. The notable thing is understanding what you're getting out of it—and whether that aligns with what you're hoping to achieve.

“I want women to feel empowered to choose exercise based on what they enjoy and what actually works,” says Ritchey.

For someone primarily focused on building muscle, Ritchey recommends treating sculpt classes as opportunities for cardio or simply enjoyable movement, rather than as a replacement for progressive strength training.

They can even be great options for off days from lifting. “I don’t want to discourage anyone from moving,” she indicates. “But at the same time, we deserve to understand what is marketing and what our bodies actually respond to. We are all busy and tired and stressed [and] I want women to know how to best use their efforts to match their goals.”.

In a recent development, appreciate the workout for what it is, understand what it isn't, and choose what works for you. That, in fact, is the true artistry of exercise.

In a recent development, natalia Mehlman Petrezela, PhD, is a professor of history at the New School and author of Fit Nation: The Gains and Pains of America’s Exercise Obsession. Shannon Ritchey, PT, DPT, is a physical therapist, fitness instructor, and founder of Evlo Fitness. Laura Girard, CPT, is a NASM-certified personal trainer, founder of The Energy Academy, and co-host of the Fit Literate podcast.

Kristine Thomason is a writer and editor with over a decade of experience creating content for print and digital publications. Previously, she was the health and fitness director at mindbodygreen, and the fitness and wellness editor at Women’s Health. Kristine's work has appeared in Men's Health, Travel + Leisure, Health, and Refinery29, among others. She holds a journalism degree from Latest York University, and is certified in personal training by the National Academy of Sports Medicine (NASM).

Ray Nicholson Is Smiling Through It All

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • Recent findings suggest that “I’M RUNNING PURELY off of fumes and caffeine,” Ray Nicholson states, with a glimmer in his eye and the end of his mouth curled into a slight grin.
  • Recent findings suggest that that grin, it turns out, is a weapon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

Recent findings suggest that “I’M RUNNING PURELY off of fumes and caffeine,” Ray Nicholson states, with a glimmer in his eye and the end of his mouth curled into a slight grin. He points to a half-finished iced coffee sitting in front of him and nods his head. “It’s good.”.

Recent findings suggest that that grin, it turns out, is a weapon. It’s a smile that, somehow, employs both his dimples and furrowed brow just as much as his mouth and teeth. It’s the kind of smile that stops you in your tracks when he flashes it in the middle of a sentence. It’s also got a kill count on-screen, evoking something different in each context. Whether he’s cutting the tension in a war drama, like in his latest movie, Netflix’s The Mosquito Bowl; or making single frames into nightmares, as in Smile 2; or playing an unhinged stalker in Borderline or an unstable boyfriend in I Love You Forever—it’s clear Nicholson knows what he’s doing with that thing.

Industry observers note that it’s also a familiar grin, because it’s virtually identical to a rather iconic one: that of his father, Jack Nicholson, whose smile has been on display in timeless performances in movies like The Shining and One Flew over the Cuckoo’s Nest. You know the smile I’m talking about.

And today? Nicholson the younger is putting that grin to a latest use: namely, masking whatever else is going on inside as he glugs away at that coffee and tries to make it through a couple of grueling days of press, press, press. “It’s somewhere between hypnosis, interrogation, and a Miss America pageant,” he claims with a laugh, as the smile flashes again.

According to recent reports, the Mosquito Bowl, which comes from director Peter Berg (Friday Night Lights, Lone Survivor), follows a group of soldiers whose college football rivalries evolve into a close-knit brotherhood on the World War II battlefield. It’s based on the true story of a football game (the titular Mosquito Bowl) that was actually played. The film is based on a book of the same name by Friday Night Lights author Buzz Bissinger.

If Nicholson is tired, one would never know. It’s not just the smile, though of course that doesn’t hurt. To me, he seems excited, unafraid of diving into stories about filming The Mosquito Bowl in Australia and bonding with costars Bill Skarsgård, Nicholas Galitzine, and Tom Francis over hours of daily football and military drill training.

In a recent development, this all feels like a natural fit for Nicholson, who played football in high school and planned to play at Boston College until a run-in with MRSA cut that dream short. His performance and his relationship with his costars make the movie. But there’s more than that. In his career thus far—and in our conversation—Nicholson has proved himself as someone who’s got a certain type of charisma that pops off the screen, an inherently watchable face, a screen presence that simply can’t be taught. It’s almost as if it’s in his genes.

Recent findings suggest that MEN’S HEALTH: You have a penchant for playing very intense roles. Why do you think that is?

In a recent development, RAY NICHOLSON: It’s interesting. As a young actor… It’s sort of what you get. You know what I mean? I guess I have an intense face. I guess I’m intense. But ultimately, the challenge of becoming an artist is learning how to put 100 percent of your heart and soul into something and not leave anything behind. That’s the only way I feel comfortable on camera, and that’s the joy of doing it. I find fulfillment in that hole in the soul when I have that intensity. The mundane is more difficult for me; I’m trying to learn how to enjoy that.

MH: Your character, Tony, in The Mosquito Bowl, is a normal guy, more or less, but he’s in this extraordinary situation. Did it feel like a bit of fresh air to get to take on that kind of role compared to something like Smile 2, for example?

RN: Yeah. On Smile 2, I was very much a day player. But it never really shifts. Ultimately, I’m there to be of service. Especially in Smile 2, Naomi [Scott] is acting her ass off all day, and they might have three seconds for one shot I’m doing all day, and I might have been there for 14 hours, but it doesn’t matter. I’m there for a day, and just to be there and be good vibes.

But this, we were there every single day. I’m glad I learned so much from Pete and Bill. As an artist, as a human being, I learned how to have grace with the cards I was dealt. I was dealt very beautiful cards, but you can play a good hand very poorly. I think I’ve finally found grace with my circumstance.

MH: Did shooting on location in Australia help you feel immersed?

RN: For sure. We were all away from family—all we had was each other. Which was really beautiful and a challenge, but exactly what it needed. And when you get a script like that, all that brotherhood is baked in and then all you need is buy-in. And we fell in love with each other. Me, Tom, and Bill, we’ve traveled the world. We went to the African World Cup final. They’re my best friends. I think about them every day. It’s amazing to think I didn’t know them before this, and now they’re people I think of every single day. We shot all outdoors, all sequentially, in order.

According to recent reports, RN: Insanely rare. It’s insanely rare, because it makes it so much easier. I know how I felt, because I did it yesterday.

MH: Can you tell me about your relationship with football? Obviously, it makes sense with this movie.

According to recent reports, RN: The first sport I played was basketball. I grew up a really chubby kid. I was not cool. And my sister was the most popular, beautiful girl in elementary school, and I was the fat nerdy brother that liked Yu-Gi-Oh! and whatever.

RN: Yu-Gi-Oh! was sick, objectively. And I played Pokémon. When I was about 9 years old, I was really overweight, so I found AAU basketball. I remember my first practice, I was jogging around and I literally tripped over half court and these guys picked me up. That was the first time I felt something like that. Then, when I got a little bit older, I played Pop Warner. And, once again, I was a bit chubbier, but I was fast and I had a good arm. I wanted to play quarterback, they wanted me to play offensive line. And then I became this chubby Michael Vick, trucking other kids [Laughs]. Kind of a beast. And that was the first time I felt confident.

RN: I’m confident between these lines. And I could be angry. My anger was always so self-directed. I had so much shame. That was the first place I was like, “Ah, I can express this.” That’s a really key thing for kids.

In a recent development, I was very happy, a reporter in one of my Zoom interviews was like, “You averaged 8.94 yards a carry. You want to tell them what that means?” I was like, “That means I was fucking good!” [Laughs].

According to recent reports, RN: It was the first thing that gave me confidence, and you have that feeling of family. And you have that tough love. You have this love through discipline and through pain, but that’s the love between men. That was so crucial to me, and that saved my life. It came into my life exactly when I needed it, and I really struggled when I lost it. I got a staph infection that turned into MRSA. My arm was so inflamed, they drew a line on my arm and were like, “If the infection gets past here [points to biceps], we’re cutting your arm off.” I lost 50 pounds in a week.

Sources indicate that RN: My senior year of high school. I thought I was going to go to Boston College and play football. Not on scholarship, but I went to the camp and they were like, “You could be a deferred walk-on,” or whatever. I thought I was going to be like Jerry Maguire—that’s what I wanted to do. I came out of this semi-comatose thing and I was like, “I want to be an actor. I’m just so scared. I’m just so fucking scared.” And then I just slowly dipped my toe in. I’m glad everything’s happening now, because I have the head on my shoulders to handle it.

MH: You went through something really tough.

RN: Yeah. If I was a kid, I don’t even know if I would be alive, to be honest with you. I’m so grateful that it happened on a bigger plan than on mine. A lot of the things I was originally attracted to would coil like a flame hat now. It’s all a major blessing.

MH: What was it like working with Peter Berg?

RN: Bill and I are used to growing up with eccentric men, you know what I mean? We kind of understand it. It’s one of those things where, with eccentric men, it requires you to butt heads and be like, “I didn't like that, but I like you.” You know what I mean? Bill’s always like, “You’re Pete’s favorite son. You guys fight, but he loves you the most.” We really had this familial thing. Bill was the older brother, Nick and I were the middle brothers, and Tom was the little brother.

It has been revealed that we all worked so hard, and we wanted to fight for what was best. I really respect Pete. I love him as a filmmaker. I love him as a man. I really respect him as a leader, because you’re going to meet him exactly where he’s at. And I respect that. I think conflict is where art is made. We’re too conflict averse, and I really admire Pete for his style and his honesty.

MH: When you’ve gone through this kind of experience, how do you come down afterward when it’s time to go home?

RN: There’s this mourning process. The last week of filming, we were all crying. The cast was crying, the crew was crying, makeup was crying. It was really intense. And we fell in love with the experience and we fell in love with each other. Before Bill met us, he went to Okinawa. And he actually took a charcoal etching of the gravestones of Tony Butkovich, Bob Bauman, and Dave Schreiner, and he gave them to us on the last day. And we all were tearing up and we wrote a letter to each other and to the men that we played. I think part of it was you have to let go.

Sources indicate that it took me a while to go home—I didn’t go straight home. Me and Tom went to Sydney and just hung out at the beach with some friends we had made there. We went to go see Oasis.

RN: For sure. But also, it’s like you have this fear of do we really love each other or were we just working on this project? It’s been really cool in the months since we started shooting to see how our relationships have developed. We’ll always have The Mosquito Bowl.

Sources indicate that RN: It just took a while for me to get home. I really relish being alone. I really needed time to reset. I went through a breakup right when I got home. I almost took six months off, not even looking for a job. I finished writing the script I wanted to do, but I really just took some time. I always have to take time to be like, “What am I if I’m not acting?” And that’s a hard thing.

MH: What was your wake-up point of, like, “Okay, time to get back to it”?

RN: I finished that script and I was like, “Well, I’m not a writer!” I’m really proud of what I did, but I think it was just like, “Oh.” We were getting closer to press, and I was like, “Oh, geez.” Like, “Oh god, should I have done a job already?”.

MH: And what’s it like at this stage in the process?

According to recent reports, RN: Going into press, Bill and I were like, “We’re not going to see the final cut. We’re promoting purely on good vibes. We’ve fucking got this.” And we watched it during the premiere, and I cried. I was so happy. I was so proud of how it turned out.

Industry observers note that we were talking about feeling like frauds. I think if someone handed me a script and was like, “Here, you play Ray Nicholson,” I’d be like, “You could probably find somebody better.” There’s always that fraudulent thing, and we all feel it, and that’s the beauty of it. It comes and goes. Now I feel a little bit better about what’s coming next, because I feel really proud of this movie.

MH: How do you think about the future?

Sources indicate that RN: I look forward to more opportunities with more filmmakers I love and respect. I also operate from a place of faith that the right thing will come.My dad’s my hero. I think he’s magic. I love him more than anything. When I was first doing a Meisner exercise and you’re knocking, coming through the door, I was comparing myself to, Is that worthy of three Oscars and a 50-year career? So much of my practice has just been learning to be present. And so now I have less moments when I’m in my car driving, crying, thinking about I’m getting an Oscar, and my dad... And that’s a good thing. I’ve just gotten way more present about it.

I’m also open to the idea that this might not be right for me. The world might take me in another direction. I was really closed off to that before. Because I thought that if I didn’t do something, I was unworthy of my life. I think a lot of that is just therapy. And I’m finding the real joy in it.

In a recent development, I lost football and I was really lost in my life, and I didn’t know what to do. Acting has slowly become the thing that saves my life. It’s not only what gives me a purpose, but it’s the tool I meet myself with. I don’t know who the hell I am. I don’t really remember anything from my life. And then somehow, when I read a script, I’m like, “Oh, that is you.” When I first started, I didn’t really have those kind of goals. I don’t want to say because it’s bullshit, but that’s the industry. That’s beautiful, and I love the industry, but I’m more focused on how I approach every day.

Sources indicate that RN: That was the key thing, and that’s all personal life stuff. But the key is being of service, and I believe that ultimately, I’m in the service industry. When I think about my dad, he makes me smile every time I see him on-screen. I want some kid somewhere to smile every time he sees me.

It has been revealed that MH: Last question. Do you have a favorite or most rewatched movie of your dad’s?

According to recent reports, RN: It’s tough. I’m a sucker. It’s like every PTA or Kubrick movie you watch, you’re like, “That’s my favorite.” I didn’t watch my dad’s movies until I was 18. I love Cuckoo’s Nest. I love The Shining. I always come back to The Last Detail. For some reason, I really fucking love that movie. I think it’s because he loves it so much and he’s like, “It’s underappreciated.” So I’m like, “But I love it, Dad!” I love watching his movies. It’s a cool thing, and I want my kid to watch my movies someday.

Sources indicate that RN: I just want to make people happy and smile. And break their hearts a little bit.

GM just made it way easier for EV drivers to charge at Electrify America stations

  • Industry observers note that chevrolet, Cadillac, and GMC EV drivers enrolled in GM’s Energy Pass can now simply plug in to an Electrify America station to start charging.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

In a recent development, when Jennifer Lawrence joined Instagram in September, fans rejoiced at the idea of seeing more content from the actress known for her sarcastic humor and likable authenticity. What we didn’t see coming was the launch of her new hair care brand Mes° Beauty (pronounced “mess”) and the public backlash that followed.

In an already oversaturated beauty market, celebrity brands are a dime a dozen, and the announcement of Mes° Beauty didn’t exactly land well with the public. “She saw the numbers Rihanna, Selena Gomez, and Hailey Bieber were pulling in, and suddenly decided to join Instagram, too. Not necessarily to connect with her audience, but perhaps to tap into the same commercial machine and sell us even more stuff,” wrote one Instagram commenter.

According to recent reports, JLaw teamed up with Jasmina Aganovic, founder of biotech beauty company Arcaea Labs, to formulate the brand’s hair care. As they say, the proof is in the pudding, so when I was sent all three products in a PR mailer, I knew I wanted to put them to the test.

Read my full, honest review of Mes° Beauty’s hair mask, serum, and volume mist below.

An intensive repair mask designed to be applied to dry hair anytime before washing. The milky-colored mask has a silky yet sticky, gelatin-like consistency that clings to your hair as you apply it. According to the brand, the mask prevents breakage and wash-day protein loss and protects the hair’s lipid barrier.

According to recent reports, the Multitask Repair Mask differs from other hair masks because you apply it before shampooing and can leave it on for five minutes or overnight. With such a wide treatment time, it might take some trial and error to find the “sweet spot” for your hair type. During my testing, I applied a generous coat of the mask 5 to 10 minutes before shampooing. The second time, I tried applying a thinner coat of the mask, then pinned my hair up with a claw clip for about two hours before rinsing it out. The longer you wear it, the better the results. I would recommend applying a light coat before going about your day; that way, the scent isn’t overpowering and it won’t drip on your clothes.

Recent findings suggest that after just two uses, my hair looked shinier and felt more hydrated after styling. As someone who rarely prepares my hair care routine ahead of time, I appreciate that I can apply the mask just five minutes before I hop in the shower and still get noticeable results.

Although Mes° states the mask doubles as a styler for a glossy wet-hair look, I wouldn’t use it in that way. I think the product's consistency is too sticky and would be uncomfortable and messy (literally) to wear all day.

Some reviewers have mentioned a slightly off-putting smell. While the scent doesn’t bother me (it smells like a light, musky fragrance), it may not be for everyone. If I’m paying $52 for a hair mask, it would be nice to have a luxurious fragrance to add to the experience. If a brand is going to do musk, really lean into it with notes of sandalwood, amber, or patchouli.

In a recent development, the packaging also makes the product difficult to use. In the mailer I received, the mask comes in a GoGo Squeez-like pouch that you’re supposed to empty into the plastic tub. However, dipping my fingers into the tub felt clumsy, and next time I would just dispense directly from the pouch.

A bi-phase serum that smooths frizz, restores shine, and provides heat protection up to 450 degrees Fahrenheit. The “bi-phase” claim comes from combining a lightweight oil and a serum in the formula. After touching it, applying it, and letting it sit in my hair for a few days, I think calling it a serum is misleading. The consistency and the way it applies are much more like a hair oil.

On day two hair, I warmed two drops of the Off-Duty Restyling Serum between my palms, and worked it through my strands. I have very thick, straight, shoulder-length hair, so when I applied the serum up through my mid-lengths, it was way too oily. I don’t know if I would use it to restyle my hair unless I was planning to use a hot tool.

In a recent development, I also tested the serum as a finishing product, applying it to my ends after blow-drying. I found this to be the most effective way to use the product on my hair type.

It has been revealed that overall, the Off-Duty Restyling Serum doesn’t make much sense to me. What’s the point of having heat protection if it’s made for “reshaping yesterday’s style?” Are we going back in with more heat? To me, that sounds like an extra step in my morning routine that I do not have the time or patience for.

Sources indicate that on days when I wash and blow-dry my hair, I like using a tiny amount of the serum just on my ends, and I've found it dries down nicely and leaves my hair soft and touchable. That noted, I own other lightweight hair oils that work just as well for a fraction of the price—like FromLabs’ Protein Capsule Hair Repair Oil. If you have fine, wavy, or curly hair, the Off-Duty Serum may work better for you.

According to recent reports, A lightweight spray that reduces scalp oiliness for lasting lift. Instead of creating gritty texture or absorbing excess oil like a dry shampoo, the Good Roots mist helps balance the scalp microbiome to produce less oil at the roots, extending the time until your next wash.

Over the past two weeks, I tested the Good Roots mist in three ways: applying it to damp hair before blow-drying, applying it to damp hair before air-drying, and applying it to dry day-two and day-three hair.

After about five uses of trial and error, I found it worked best when I applied it to my clean, damp roots and blow-dried. The heat felt like it helped dry down and “activate” the mist, whereas letting my hair air-dry didn’t produce much volume.

Recent findings suggest that pro-Tip: Be sure to hold the bottle about a foot away for even misting. The applicator pump doesn’t produce a fine spritz, and it took me a few uses to get that right.

In a recent development, after two weeks of testing, the Good Roots Volume Mist is my favorite of the trio. Two key ingredients, the proprietary Arc-5 Technology and the Mediterranean microalgae, help support a balanced scalp, keeping your hair fresher longer. With consistent use, the Good Roots mist extended my time between hair washes—I typically wash every other day, but I was able to go a third day. Plus, the Juniperus virginiana oil in the formula has a fresh, woody scent that reminds me of a fancy sea salt spray.

I also like that the mist doesn’t make my hair feel super gritty or textured the way a dry shampoo might. That noted, I have other dry shampoo products that do a lot more heavy lifting than this volume mist. If I’m looking to achieve noticeable volume and lift in my thick hair, the Good Roots mist doesn’t cut it.

It has been revealed that my general critique of Mes° Beauty is that the products are not very intuitive. They seem straightforward, but the brand doesn’t give great direction on how to get the most out of them. After the first one or two uses, you may feel they barely do anything at all. But if you learn how to use them properly when styling your hair, they can perform fairly well.

Mes° is supposed to be about “Less time fixing your hair. More time living,” but in reality, achieving that effortlessly chic, tousled look requires a fair bit of effort. In my opinion, this lineup is much more suited to someone who blows out or flat irons or curls their hair once or twice a week and wants to extend their style. For my hair type, these products don’t fit into my routine in a way that makes sense, but if you have fine and/or wavy hair, they might work better for you.

Curious about my other hair standbys? They’re currently $30 and under—and make for excellent beauty gift ideas for your loved ones for the upcoming holiday season.

Industry News: I Wore the Nike Alphafly 4 Super Shoes to Run a Marathon. Here’s What I Thought.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved.
  • THE WORLD OF elite running moves fast.
  • Sources indicate that the Swoosh’s last pinnacle racer, the Alphafly 3, was unveiled all the way back in November 2023 (the late Kelvin Kiptum broke the marathon world record wearing a prototype of the model at the Chicago Marathon earlier that year).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that our product picks are editor-tested, expert-approved. We may earn a commission through links on our site. Why Trust Us?

THE WORLD OF elite running moves fast. That might seem an obvious observation, sure—but it applies beyond the athletes chasing finish lines to the gear they use for peak performance. So as world records fell and mass race participation swelled over the last few years, hardcore running shoe lovers wondered: Where is Nike, and what’s taking so long to unleash the brand’s next top-level super shoe?

Sources indicate that the Swoosh’s last pinnacle racer, the Alphafly 3, was unveiled all the way back in November 2023 (the late Kelvin Kiptum broke the marathon world record wearing a prototype of the model at the Chicago Marathon earlier that year). While the shoe has been a massively popular race day pick for all kinds of runners from 2024 on, other brands entered the super shoe space Nike originated and put out light, fast racers that offered speedier specs and took podium places (including a latest marathon world record, the first sub-2-hour finish that bested even Eliud Kipchoge’s 2019 exhibition run in an earlier Alphafly model). Nike put out some great releases in the interim, including the excellent Vomero Plus and Premium models—but the top echelon of the racing line remained untouched.

After a nearly three-year gap, the Alphafly 4 is here. I got my feet in a pair ahead of its October 29 launch and my fall race, the NYC Marathon, so I put the super shoe to the test on the city’s streets for 26.2 miles (and a few more along the training cycle) to see if it lives up to the Alphafly name.

THE ALPHAFLY 4 builds on the same design language as its predecessor, with two of Nike’s signature Air Zoom units in the forefoot, a high stack of ZoomX foam, and a carbon fiber plate. But there are new updates that have helped to make the shoe—at least according to Nike—lighter and more efficient.

Sources indicate that the latest version of the Atomknit upper is a fine mesh that’s more substantial than it looks. Unlike some other top-end super shoes, Nike didn’t skimp on the outsole, with plenty of rubber coverage on the bottom. The carbon fiber plate is wider, too, and the shoe overall is roomier than previous iterations.

According to recent reports, still, the Alphafly 4 weighs in at about 6.6 ounces, which is on the lighter end for a mainline racing shoe (but not the lightest on the market). The foam formulation is also upcoming; the top layer is called ZoomX LT, which Nike claims is lighter and provides more energy return than the standard ZoomX, which is below the plate. That foam is stacked to 39 mm, with an 8 mm drop.

AS I BEGAN my NYC marathon run, I could feel the Alphafly 4’s combination of plate, foam, and rocker ramping up underfoot for a fast day. The push off the pavement was effortless, and the combination of the perfect weather and unmatched vibes of the crowd made it easy to surge ahead of my target pace. But I wasn’t gunning for a PR (this was my third major race of the year, and I was more focused on maintaining a balanced pace and testing the self-serve water stations than pushing my limits).

I dialed back my excitement as I crossed the Verrazzano Bridge from the start on Staten Island, a spot that’s notorious for gassing overhyped runners leading off the race, and I was able to settle into a comfortable groove. The Alphafly 4 brought a good balance; I felt it was somewhere between the ultra-propulsive super shoes that have lately dominated the elite racing circuit and the more approachable carbon plate shoes that aren’t able to quite keep up.

As I continued along the course, I was pleased with the consistent ride. I wasn’t exerting a ton of energy through my stride, but I was still cruising through the miles. The grippy outsole paid off as I sloshed through the water stations area, crunching crushed cups without altering my gait. I was able to just cycle my legs from step to step, allowing the rebound to push me forward.

When I ran the Boston Marathon earlier in the year, one of my biggest challenges was the pounding my feet took on the back end of the course. I was in pain for days after, and lost my first ever toenail. As I pushed through Mile 20 and above during my NYC run, I kept expecting the pain to come. While my legs did grow heavy and my pace dropped off, my feet didn’t experience the same amount of punishment. The Alphafly 4 isn’t specifically meant for folks with wide feet by any means, but the wider base was much kinder to my tired dogs than other models I’ve worn for 26.2. I finished the race on a high note pushing for the final stretch, propelled along in part thanks to the extra push I could depend on from the shoe.

Recent findings suggest that THE ALPHAFLY 4 will be a reliable racer for lots of runners who want speed on the roads without going to the extremes. I appreciated the comfortable fit and smooth ride through my own race, and the propulsion provided a nice balance between less aggressive super shoes and the pace-pushing pinnacle “hyper” shoes that have started to emerge, like Puma’s Fast-R Nitro 3, Adidas’ record-breaking Pro Evo 3, and Nike’s own Apex model, which took the top spot at the NYC marathon and replaces the Alphafly line at the top of the brand’s racing stable.

Still, less experienced runners and those who expect to take four or more hours to finish a marathon might find this to be a bit too much shoe. There are other options that will both be less expensive and friendlier to slower paces. The $280 price puts the Alphafly 4 just $5 more than the comparable Adidas Adios Pro 5 (and it’s actually $5 less at launch than the Alphafly 3). Now that there are more levels of quality for super shoes, rather than just one premier shoe per brand, costs closer to $300 seem to be the norm.

In a recent development, overall, Nike has done a solid job continuing the Alphafly legacy—there are just way more super-powered racers around now than in the early days of super shoes. Still, the model is going to work for lots of runners. If you’re chasing a goal time and you need something that can be both fast and wearable, the Alphafly 4 is going to be one of your absolute top picks.

Sources indicate that brett Williams, NASM-CPT, PES, a senior editor at Men's Health, is a certified trainer and former pro football player and tech reporter. You can find his work elsewhere at Mashable, Thrillist, and other outlets.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There are a few covetable luxury goods you’ll see pop up again and again in AD’s home tours: a Moccamaster coffee maker, a Nordic Knots rug, and Mauviel copper cookware, to name a few. As seen in this Sag Harbor home, this Parisian pied-à-terre, this Westchester residence, and this Connecticut country retreat, Mauviel is something of a status symbol in kitchens. Much like a Le Creuset Dutch oven out on display, spying a few copper pans from the French brand hanging from a rail signals that “Great Taste Lives Here.” And this week marks a good opportunity to join the club, with Mauviel sets and individual pieces up to 30% off for Black Friday at Williams Sonoma and on Shop.

According to recent reports, I’m a recent convert; I bought my Mauviel frying pan mostly to elevate the aesthetic of my kitchen, with a suspicion that the tool would also function as a fantastic piece of cookware, particularly for my beloved morning ritual of frying up an egg for breakfast. Of course it does. Unlike some of my ceramic pans that catch and dry out an egg, the Mauviel has given me no trouble, delivering me the most perfect eggs to date I’ve ever cooked. Even against my stainless-steel pans (which I do love very much), these heat a bit more promptly and evenly.

That excellent cooking capability is largely due to the construction and craftsmanship of the goods, which have a long history as a French culinary staple. Mauviel has made copper cookware since 1830 in Villedieu-les-Poêles, a town in Normandy with an enduring history of copper manufacturing; the pieces are still handcrafted there. As far as their makeup, the M’150 B pieces are, for example, 1.5 millimeters thick and constructed of a 90% polished copper exterior and a 10% stainless-steel interior. They heat evenly; are immediately responsive to heat adjustments; and work on gas, electric, and ceramic cooktops.

The pans partners with a copper kettle on the stove in this Portland manse by Jessica Helgerson.

The copper treasures do, however, require care. They’re not nonstick pots and pans, so you need a little oil or butter to get any slip. They’re hand-wash only, and Mauviel advises against using them for long stretches on high heat or leaving them empty on a hot burner. I don’t polish mine, simply because I don’t own any copper polish. The wear shows promptly, and I like that, though if AD were shooting my house, maybe I’d like it less.

Sources indicate that the Black Friday markdowns run across the line: my copper fry pan is going for $280 in the 10-inch size (25% off), a 2.5-quart sauce pan is $450 (29% off), and a 15-piece cookware set is $3,000 (32% off). For anyone who cooks every day, it’s a hard gift to beat. I, for one, now can’t imagine frying my eggs any other way.
