Letter from the Editor-in-Chief: The Good and the Hard of Life on GLP-1s

📅 23 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Healthline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, “Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more.
  • Recent findings suggest that in June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects.
  • It has been revealed that jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, “Years of diets that worked for a couple of months, then gave all the weight back and more. Now the food noise has gone quiet,” a GLP-1 user shared.

Recent findings suggest that in June, our brilliant News team published a piece about actor Mayim Bialik and her challenging experience with GLP-1 side effects. It did well, like many of the celebrity + health condition + human-interest angle features we create tend to do with our audience (that’s you all reading this!). Not a massive viral hit by any measure, but a strong performer on the traffic front.

Life in a busy newsroom went on.

It has been revealed that jump forward nearly 4 months; our equally brilliant social media team posts the piece on Facebook, leading with one of Bialik’s quotes from the article: “GLP-1s have helped people in serious need. Of that I am certain. But nobody talks much about what happens when it goes wrong.”.

It has been revealed that the fuse was lit. Nearly 12k likes, 1k reposts, and 3.5k comments later, the team had their most engaged post of the year by some margin. The irony is not lost on me that Bialik’s quote, about how rarely people talk about side effects, sparked such a deep conversation about that very thing.

GLP-1s are a substantial topic for Healthline. They drive traffic, they drive revenue, and they offer a rich seam of human-centric storytelling for our teams. Even so, no one predicted the post would catch fire the way it did. Our social team’s read is that a few things stacked up: Mayim Bialik is a name our Facebook audience knows, the topic is one where nearly everyone has a stake, and a busy thread tends to get shown to more people, who then add more comments. That’s the hypothesis. What we’ve consistently seen is that posts that lead with a quote get more people talking than those that lead with a headline. You may have noticed this article takes the same approach.

According to recent reports, we also know that the comment sections on social media aren’t always the most hospitable of environments, particularly in the health space. What stood out about the lion’s share of the comments we read was how constructive the discourse was. People were leading with deeply personal and often moving perspectives about the life changing impact (for good and bad) of GLP-1s. In turn, they were met with equally balanced and thoughtful responses.

According to recent reports, many of the comments expanded on Bialik’s experience, detailing long and difficult battles with a range of side effects. But plenty told the other side of the story: years of failed diets and struggles with chronic conditions leading to despondency, side effects that went on to ease with time, and life changing results that were ultimately worth the cost.

It has been revealed that the line that opened this piece could have come from any of those commenters. It didn’t. It came from Kitty Hough, who is 75 and lives in London. Eagle-eyed readers will have spotted that she has the same surname as me – that’s because she’s my mom. She’s one of two people closer to the Healthline home who spoke to me for this piece and whose stories echo the Facebook post thread, with the good and the hard bits side by side.

Recent findings suggest that kitty was a hockey player and distance runner as a girl, the kind who could eat what she liked without it showing. Then came children, and a weight that crept up year after year, with decades of diets that “worked for a couple of months only to be back to my former weight and then some.” In late 2024, after a lot of research, she decided to try tirzepatide.

Since then, Kitty has lost 56 pounds. She indicates her joints hurt less, which she puts down to reduced inflammation. She is more mobile. The constant chatter about food has faded. She thinks harder before she eats now.

Sources indicate that “I am a strong believer that obesity is a disease and in my case certainly not the result of overindulgence or laziness,” she says. “GLP-1s have greatly improved my health and self-esteem. After years of struggling with my weight, I have finally found a way to solve the problem.”.

Kitty will also tell you what it cost. Nausea. Constipation. Sulfur-tasting burps and rough nights of indigestion. Initial hair loss that has since grown back, and loose skin. Muscle loss. And she misses some of the true joy of cooking and eating food.

It has been revealed that but despite bumps in her journey, Kitty remains convinced that the benefits of GLP-1s for her life and health outweigh any drawbacks she’s experienced. “I am conscious that I will probably be on this drug for a long time if not for life. It is truly a miracle drug.”.

I also spoke to Ann Marie Maguire, AGNP-C, RN, TCTCN, a nurse practitioner specializing in transplantation and cellular therapy, the sister of Healthline’s Chief Business Officer Christine Macguire, and someone who has lost over 50lbs since starting GLP-1s in 2022.

Recent findings suggest that “I struggled with my weight since my teens and always believed I should be able to manage it on my own. But in my 30s, my knees were hurting just getting out of bed or walking to dinner. I realized how much my weight was affecting my quality of life. Starting a GLP-1 in 2022, alongside healthier eating and exercise, made a tremendous difference. My only regret is not starting sooner,” said Ann Marie.

As a healthcare professional, Ann Marie also identified cost as a major factor that can’t be ignored regarding GLP-1s and their impact.

Industry observers note that “There’s understandable debate about the long-term use and cost of these medications,” she says. “But we also need to consider the health and financial burden of obesity, including cardiovascular complications, hospitalizations, surgeries and ongoing medications. The cost conversation should account for the potential benefits of preventing or reducing those complications.”.

In a recent development, ann Marie points to a frustration many patients will recognize: reaching a healthier weight can become the reason coverage gets cut off. “We don’t automatically stop blood pressure medication because a patient’s readings improve,” she says. The treatment may be what’s keeping the condition controlled. Obesity, she argues, deserves the same approach. “Reaching a goal weight can mean treatment is working, and decisions about continuing it should reflect the patient’s ongoing needs, benefits and side effects.”.

It’s notable to note that this article looks at the experiences of only a handful of people out of the millions who now take GLP-1s. Like all drugs, these medications are not right for everyone. Side effects are common; some of them can be serious, and both the long-term impact and what happens when people stop are still being worked out. Ultimately, your care team, with knowledge of your medical history, is a far better guide than a comment thread.

Yet the evidence now reaches well beyond the scales: large trials have linked semaglutide to fewer heart attacks and strokes in people with heart disease and slower kidney decline in people with diabetes and kidney disease, and tirzepatide became the first FDA-approved drug for moderate to severe sleep apnea in adults with obesity.

In a recent development, stories like Kitty’s, Ann Marie’s, Mayim Bialik’s, and those of the 3.5k commenters on the Facebook post aren’t proof of what will happen to you one way or another. But for a lot of people, my mom included, these drugs have changed what an ordinary day looks like, and in many cases changed what their future can look like.

It has been revealed that one of the most significant drug developments of the century so far? Hard to argue with.

Robin Hough is the Editor-in-Chief of Healthline, and in addition to this regular Letter from the Editor column, he can be found every other Wednesday in our Healthline Wellness Wire newsletter.

Breaking: The 11 Best War Movies About Brotherhood, Ranked

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that DIRECTOR PETER BERG had never made a World War II movie before The Mosquito Bowl, but he certainly knows a thing or two about football.
  • Berg’s new Netflix film dramatizes the stories of football players John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson), Bob Bauman (Bill Skarsgård), and Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis), who traded the NFL draft for military service.
  • In a recent development, the Mosquito Bowl underlines the devastating impact WWII’s casualty count had on an entire generation of young athletes, and the film unites its twin focuses of war and football by their mutual sense of brotherhood.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that DIRECTOR PETER BERG had never made a World War II movie before The Mosquito Bowl, but he certainly knows a thing or two about football. The director of Friday Night Lights has returned to a world of cocksure young players with their whole lives ahead of them in dire need of rousing their morale—only now it’s the true story of the football game between two World War II Marine regiments at Guadalcanal on Christmas Eve 1944. There’s another connection: both The Mosquito Bowl and Friday Night Lights are adapted from books by author Buzz Bissinger.

Berg’s new Netflix film dramatizes the stories of football players John McLaughry (Nicholas Galitzine), Tony Butkovich (Ray Nicholson), Bob Bauman (Bill Skarsgård), and Dave Schreiner (Tom Francis), who traded the NFL draft for military service. After enduring years of the Pacific campaign, they realize how valuable the team spirit and camaraderie of football can be as the Battle of Okinawa looms ahead of them.

In a recent development, the Mosquito Bowl underlines the devastating impact WWII’s casualty count had on an entire generation of young athletes, and the film unites its twin focuses of war and football by their mutual sense of brotherhood. The deeply felt connection between soldiers is the lifeblood of historical war films; when done convincingly, a squad’s well-earned devotion and loyalty add rich melodrama to the action. Brotherhood is just as compelling when it is subverted—like the respect felt between soldiers on opposing sides, or when hardened, broken combatants struggle to express the empathy and compassion they feel. The best war movies know that brotherhood endures after the fighting stops, but in different forms—softer, stranger, when it’s hard to reconcile the memories of war with a world that continues as normal.

To mark the Thanksgiving release of The Mosquito Bowl on Netflix, we ranked the most gripping and rousing war films about brotherhood.

Sources indicate that an ensemble of actors you'd typically see in a "Young Stars of Tomorrow" profile immerse themselves in a U.S. Navy SEAL platoon and recreate a real-time Iraq War firefight that co-director Ray Mendoza was a part of. Opening with the platoon jubilantly dancing to "Call On Me" streamed through their base's crappy internet, Warfare quickly adopts a stripped-back and meticulous play-by-play of how one slice of warfare was actually experienced. You get a sense of brotherhood from the practiced, reflexive interactions between SEALs, and their interdependence also helped build the film, as Mendoza and co-director Alex Garland drew from the testimonies of his fellow soldiers when writing the script. The stylistic choices—like a thundering sound mix and infrequent use of satellite photography—add an extra layer of tension to Warfare's depiction of courage under fire. It’s one of the most visceral movies in recent memory about modern war.

According to recent reports, before he brought us high-octane visions of robot cops and ambitious showgirls, Paul Verhoeven directed a handful of smash hits in his native Netherlands, including this Golden Globe-nominated war epic about the diverging fates of Dutch students during the Nazi occupation. Led by a supremely dashing Rutger Hauer, Soldier of Orange begins in 1938 and follows the wartime trajectory of Erik Lanshof, an initially neutral but increasingly principled aristocrat who protects his Dutch Resistance friends and distances himself from fascist collaborators. Before long, his entire school group has pledged one type of loyalty or another. Observed over a period of time, war reveals everything, and Erik’s blossoming heroism emerges as a result of his friendships all changing—for better or worse.

Forgive us for taking a creative approach to the headline so early in the list: Hell in the Pacific features no battles or squadron camaraderie, and takes place on a deserted island with only two characters—an American pilot (Lee Marvin) and a Japanese army captain (Toshiro Mifune)—who don’t understand a word the other person claims. Even without comprehension, the American and Japanese soldiers find a hundred ways to rile each other up, including shock tactics, sabotage, pranks, and even makeshift imprisonment. Gradually, they realize each other’s company is the strongest connection to their starving humanity available to them, even if they’re affected in a way they can’t explain. Free from the rhetoric and politics of war, Marvin and Mifune play men who slip into a state of brash, stubborn childishness, and a brotherly kinship forms in spite of their inherent opposition.

Recent findings suggest that clint Eastwood and Steven Spielberg sound like an odd pair to collaborate on a war picture, but Eastwood’s pared-down, melancholic visual style is a terrific fit for this post-Band of Brothers war movie. Flags of Our Fathers wasn’t received as positively as its Japanese-language companion film Letters from Iwo Jima, but it’s a robust and affecting watch—splitting its runtime between the overwhelming Battle of Iwo Jima and its aftermath, where three soldiers celebrated as the iconic “flag-raisers” spent the final year of the Pacific Campaign on a spiritually draining propaganda tour. Flags of Our Fathers takes the essential themes of war cinema—brotherhood, sacrifice, heroism—and juxtaposes them with the United States military manufacturing their own national images and narratives in real time. The tension between the brutal experience of being a brother-in-arms and the sanitized version promoted by war’s survivors makes for a powerful watch.

Industry observers note that it’s as if director David Ayer (Suicide Squad, Bright) made a WWII movie to hammer home two points: tank warfare was a nightmare, and soldier hazing was way more hardcore than what you see in Band of Brothers. In the final months of the war in Europe, Wardaddy (Brad Pitt) rolls his bloody and battered tank unit slowly toward Berlin, and the arrival of fresh-faced pencil-pusher Norman (Logan Lerman) gives the hardened squad a chance to berate and bully the newcomer about all the ways he is soft, and war is hell. As their fellow brothers-in-arms are increasingly blasted apart into viscera, Wardaddy’s take-no-shit squad bolsters their unsentimental unity, and each of the five traumatized brothers rely on each other to watch their back and keep them sane on a frontline that might as well be the border to hell.

Recent findings suggest that spike Lee’s bracing film about the scars of Vietnam takes a familiar concept—a jaded band of veterans who try to pull off a heist—and spins it in a thorny, unpredictable direction. Four older Black veterans (led by an intense, captivating, and Oscar-snubbed Delroy Lindo) return to ‘Nam to recover the CIA gold their squadron hid during the war—aside from a delayed payday, it’s also the ultimate memorial of their late squad leader Norman (Chadwick Boseman). Marked by years of bitterness and PTSD, the “Bloods” retrace their steps while juggling painful reflections on how the war left them angry and guilty. When they're ambushed in the jungle and have to pick up guns again, we're reminded that Lee is never satisfied sticking in one narrative mode for too long, but the jagged catharsis of cranky, once-loyal soldiers confronting their wounds is far more visceral to watch.

Industry observers note that when Private Alex (Harry Styles) says, “We're regimental brothers, mate,” in the belly of a fishing trawler on Dunkirk Beach, he’s not acting nobly—he’s making the case for throwing a soldier he thinks is German (he’s actually French) to the Nazis surrounding them. So much of Christopher Nolan’s war film about the perilous evacuation of Allied troops from France’s northernmost beaches centers on division: soldier feuds, breakdowns in communication, and a nonlinear narrative that takes place over a week or an hour depending on who’s in front of the camera. But Dunkirk’s staggering disaster and survival action builds to an overwhelming climactic sense of unity. Across every mini-arc and timeline, Nolan shows us countless pairs of soldiers, pilots, and civilians who stand together as symbolic brothers.

Recent findings suggest that after the famously gnarly and disorienting D-Day beach landing sequence—which has influenced every WWII action movie since, including The Mosquito Bowl—Saving Private Ryan settles into the most iconic band of brothers story outside of… well, Band of Brothers, co-created by this film’s director and star. Tom Hanks is the grouchy uncle leading a reluctant squad to rescue Private James Francis Ryan (Matt Damon) from the front lines after his brothers were killed in action. The squadron's trudge through France is fueled with banter, grumbling, and the type of resentment that stews between siblings who hate when someone receives special treatment. Steven Spielberg’s gift for balancing movie-star gravitas and off-the-cuff charisma is on full display in the ensemble, but no gruff, hot-tempered soldier has a response to Private Ryan's justification for not returning to his mom: “Tell her that when you found me, I was here, and I was with the only brothers I have left.”.

The only war film on this list to be set before the 20th century and at sea, the Napoleonic Wars-era Master and Commander has a reputation for being a “dudes/gentlemen rock” classic: the reputation still holds up. Under the command of Captain Jack Aubrey (Russell Crowe), the HMS Surprise wages war against a French frigate that taunts the crew across the seas. Majestic naval battles aside, much of Master and Commander has a warm hangout tone, focusing on the kinship between Aubrey and ship’s surgeon Maturin, their interest in classical music and botanical science, and revelrous suppers in the captain’s quarters. It's impossible to watch Peter Weir’s sea epic and not pine for the brotherly loyalty (maybe not the seasickness or cannonball attacks) that Aubrey inspires here. Nothing will make you feel the romantic thrill of adventure like Master and Commander.

Industry observers note that pick your favorite scene from The Deer Hunter: the riotous wedding party, the spontaneous Frankie Valli singalong over a game of pool, or the exacting game of Russian roulette played by prisoners of war. They each shine a light on the ordinary, working-class brotherhood that was completely transformed by the Vietnam War. This Oscar-winning epic builds complex, traumatized characters (played by Robert De Niro, John Cazale, and Christopher Walken) who reckon with never being able to experience their relationships and community in the same way again. The Deer Hunter paints such a disturbing and fragile picture of the “before and after” of Vietnam, as each brotherly bond becomes charged with alienation and despair. Notorious for its multiple “death game” sequences, The Deer Hunter excels in making its harrowing portrayal of war and PTSD genuinely heartbreaking.

In a recent development, one of the best things to come out of legendary Hong Kong filmmakers John Woo and Tsui Hark falling out was the future director of Hard Boiled and Face/Off leaving the iconic A Better Tomorrow series to make this searing war story. Beginning in the late ’60s, it focuses on three close friends (Tony Leung, Jacky Cheung, Waise Lee) whose smuggling ambitions dunk them headfirst in the brutality and desperation of the Vietnam War. Bullet in the Head blends the epic sweep of Upcoming Hollywood war epics (Apocalypse Now, The Deer Hunter) with Woo’s “heroic bloodshed” toolkit, which meant electric action spectacle and bold, tragic melodrama. An underrated operatic beast in Woo’s stacked filmography—not to mention a personal one, as Woo used the film to express his reaction to the 1989 Tiananmen Square massacre—the action is always in service of a high-stakes tri-friendship that can only take so much passion and betrayal before the treasured brotherhood breaks.

According to recent reports, rory Doherty is a critic and journalist based in Edinburgh, Scotland. His work can be found at British GQ, Vulture, Inverse, AV Club, and other publications. He can be found on Twitter/X at @roryhasopinions.

A self-assembling supramolecular nanocarrier protects Cas9 RNPs from degradation, enhances systemic delivery and preferential tumor accumulation, and enables pH-responsive intracellular release. Developed by researchers at the Institute of Science Tokyo, this platform achieved a 37.2% indel frequency at the luciferase target locus in HeLa-Luc tumor tissue in mice, compared with 1.5% with free RNPs, and suppressed tumor growth in separate mouse models. These findings support the further development of systemic CRISPR-based cancer therapies.

#98488. Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

Scientists created artificial, life-like muscles for humanoid robots

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (993 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that for better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities.
  • Sources indicate that designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat.
  • “Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang noted in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that for better or worse, some scientists seem dead set on infusing humanoid robots with more lifelike qualities. They’ve already experimented with stretching lab-grown human skin over robot faces and with a synthetic hydrogel skin that lets robots really “feel” burns and cuts. Now, a team of engineers at the University of Pennsylvania wants to dig under the skin. In a  study published this week in Advanced Functional Materials, the team describes a highly controllable artificial robot muscle inspired by the small muscles in human eyes and fingers. They put them to the test by having a robot hand strike piano keys at varying intensities and made a set of human eye muscles able to maintain a gaze. It all feels quite uncomfortably adjacent to the 1973 sci-fi film and HBO series Westworld.

Sources indicate that designing robot muscles that act like the real thing poses some engineering challenges right off the bat. For starters, most large robots today, especially humanoid ones, rely on bulky, rigid motors and components. That’s fine for more straightforward actions like walking and lifting, but recreating the muscles that move our eyes or fingers requires far more delicate precision. In this case, the engineers needed a material that prioritized flexibility and fine control while staying strong enough to hold up after repeated use. As with many aspects of robotics, tasks that seem quite easy for humans to do are actually often the most difficult tasks for machines. While bipedal robots have been pulling off dance routines and performing acrobatics worth of a Marvel superhero for years, they still fall flat when it comes to something as simple as folding laundry or holding a gaze.

“Soft robotic muscles need to be both strong and flexible to mimic human movements, but these properties are rarely found in the same material,” study co-author and University of Pennsylvania engineer Shu Yang noted in a statement.

For their muscle fiber, the team settled on liquid crystal elastomers (LCE) combined with graphene and an embedded ultrathin copper coil. The LCE, a rubber-like material, acts as the actual muscle, both contracting and stretching. The graphene serves as a reinforcer, making the material both a bit softer and tougher, so it holds up even when opposing muscles pull in other directions. Together, these two ingredients can produce movement, but on their own they struggle to stay put. When heated, the LCE stretches but then keeps contracting, eventually creeping back toward its original length as it rapidly cools. That’s a problem for subtle movements like holding a gaze or pressing a piano key with light, steady force, where the muscle needs to hold a precise position over a period of time.

That’s where the coil comes in. The team added the coil inside the fiber to serve as a kind of temperature gauge, and the sensors determine when the muscle is losing heat and contracting. With those readings, the team could then gradually increase temperature to ensure the muscle held its position.

It has been revealed that “We used the resistance of the embedded copper coil as a feedback signal and adjusted the heating power in real time to keep the resistance near a target value,” added study co-author and University of Pennsylvania Ph.D. student Xuelin Wu. “Because the coil served as both a heater and a sensor, we did not need a separate sensor for feedback.”.

With their artificial muscle designed, it was time to test it in real-world scenarios. First, the team fitted the muscles into a 3D-printed robot hand built to mimic finger movement. They then made the fingers press various piano keys at different levels of force and speed. Sensors placed on the bottom of the keys were able to tell how hard each note was played. The detached hand was no Mozart, but it worked.

In a recent development, next, they mounted a pair of robotic eyeballs on freely rotating ball joints inside 3D-printed shells. The muscle fibers were attached around the edges of opposing pairs, which were meant to mimic how muscles in the eyes stretch and contract. In testing, the eyes shifted their gaze on demand, with controlled, repeatable movements. The resulting video demonstration is both impressive and unsettling.

Recent findings suggest that the research joins a growing field of labs and companies racing to build artificial muscle systems. In 2025, Polish startup Clone Robotics took the idea to an extreme with a horrifying video of a faceless, human-sized robot dangling from a ceiling and writhing, its movements supposedly powered by synthetic muscles and a hydraulic system meant to mimic human muscles and blood vessels. They call  their creation the world’s first “musculoskeletal android.” Though it is likely that their video was more a shocking proof-of-concept than an actively working prototype, it nonetheless provides a glimpse into a potentially unsettling future where robots replace mechanical motors and actuators with more human-like muscle fibers.

In a recent development, protoclone, the world's first bipedal, musculoskeletal android. pic.twitter.com/oIV1yaMSyE.

Recent findings suggest that the University of Pennsylvania researchers say the next step is combining more of these muscles into larger, integrated systems, where dozens of small muscles have to work together to produce more natural expressions. Down the line, they’re interested in potentially using AI computer vision to coordinate those into even more complex systems. Authenticity is the point. The long-term goal, they note, is to create robots that look and feel more and more like the real thing.

“I’m excited about the possibility of using this approach to create robots that move with the same subtlety and expressiveness we see in human faces,” concluded University of Pennsylvania engineer and paper co-author Ziyun Zhang.
